West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time.
  • Industry observers note that andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening.
  • Industry observers note that everest West Ridge some days ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Industry observers note that andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Industry observers note that everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Recent findings suggest that “So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”.

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev.

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

It has been revealed that “Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”.

In a recent development, at the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

In a recent development, on their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” mentioned Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:.

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

It has been revealed that the only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Sources indicate that objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he noted.

Store Card Discount at Checkout – Pay in Full and You Keep All of It

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pay a store card’s balance in full by the first due date, and its checkout discount is yours to keep.
  • Say the clerk offers 15% off a $600 TV if you open the store’s card today.
  • That leaves you about $3 ahead of paying $600 up front.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pay a store card’s balance in full by the first due date, and its checkout discount is yours to keep. If you’d carry the purchase instead, a year of interest at the card’s rate, often above 30%, can cost as much as the discount saves. That’s still cheaper than carrying it on a typical credit card.

Say the clerk offers 15% off a $600 TV if you open the store’s card today. That’s $90 off. But pay off the remaining $510 in 12 equal monthly payments at a 30% annual percentage rate (APR), and by our math the interest comes to about $87.

That leaves you about $3 ahead of paying $600 up front. If you’d carry the TV either way, the store card is still cheaper than a general-purpose card, at the cost of a hard inquiry on your credit report. Those averaged a 25% APR in 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) found. By our math, 12 payments on $600 at that rate cost about $84 in interest, so the store card comes out about $88 ahead. Store-only cards averaged 31%, and many charge every cardholder the same rate, so strong credit won’t get you a lower one.

FICO says a hard inquiry takes less than five points off most people’s scores and stops counting after a year. If your credit is strong, a store-only card’s starting limit is typically less than half what a general-purpose card would give you, the CFPB found. So the same $510 balance takes up a bigger share of the limit. That raises your credit utilization, which can lower your score until you pay it down.

In a recent development, after the first purchase, the card is worth using only if you shop there constantly and pay it in full every month. If you shop there only now and then, a no-annual-fee card that earns 2% back on everything you buy is the better everyday card. For the store’s rewards, ask whether it also offers a co-branded card, which many substantial retailers do. It carries the store’s name but works at other stores too.

Financing that’s interest-free only if you pay in full by a deadline is deferred interest, a different deal with risks of its own.

Take the discount only on something you came to buy, and pay the card off before you charge anything else to it.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks.
  • Sources indicate that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr.
  • The winning image indicates bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

Sources indicate that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World.

The winning image indicates bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

In a recent development, “I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”.

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more notable to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Photo: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World.

Sources indicate that ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World.

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World.

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

In a recent development, these human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World.

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

Recent findings suggest that you can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum.

According to recent reports, you can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2137 w)

Latest Update: 20 Ways to Save Money as a Family – Child Care, Food & Kids’ Costs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for parents who pay for child care, it’s usually the biggest cost that comes with kids, so that’s where your family should start saving.
  • Sources indicate that child Care Aware of America puts the national average price of child care at $13,184 a year in 2025, about 10% of a two-parent household’s median income and 33% of a single parent’s.
  • Each move below cuts one of those costs and works on its own, so you can take them one bill at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for parents who pay for child care, it’s usually the biggest cost that comes with kids, so that’s where your family should start saving. Check for free public pre-K and state child care assistance before you pay full price, use tax breaks on what’s left, then cut food and kids’ costs.

Sources indicate that child Care Aware of America puts the national average price of child care at $13,184 a year in 2025, about 10% of a two-parent household’s median income and 33% of a single parent’s. Feeding more people adds up as well, and so do the clothes, gear, activities, and parties kids outgrow or ask for again every year.

Each move below cuts one of those costs and works on its own, so you can take them one bill at a time. For rent, insurance, and other bills every household pays, the ways to save money on a tight budget still apply.

Unlike a tax break, which only trims part of the bill, a free seat can take a paid year of preschool off your costs entirely.

Industry observers note that before you pay for preschool, check whether your state or city offers free public pre-K, and apply as soon as applications open, often months ahead. If you still need a paid program, compare co-op and part-day preschools, then pay with pretax money from a dependent care flexible spending account or claim the child and dependent care credit.

Read more: Free Public Pre-K Can Replace a Year of Preschool Tuition - Check Before You Pay.

Assistance helps pay the daycare bill itself, which suits a family short on cash better than a tax credit that pays back only once you file.

Industry observers note that if you work or attend school or job training, apply to your state’s child care assistance program even if you think you earn too much, and do it early, since many states keep waiting lists. For a child under 5, apply to free Head Start or Early Head Start as well.

Read more: You May Qualify for Child Care Assistance - Some States Help Middle-Class Families.

Up to a yearly limit, what you still pay for care after the free and subsidized options can come out of a dependent care account at work.

Recent findings suggest that if you pay for daycare, preschool, or day camp so you can work, enroll in your employer’s dependent care flexible spending account (FSA) at open enrollment. Money you put in skips federal income and payroll taxes, so in the 22% bracket each dollar of care costs you about 70 cents. Elect only what you’re certain to spend.

Read more: Dependent Care FSA - Pay for Daycare Before Income & Payroll Taxes.

After-school care and summer day camp can count toward the credit for kids under 13, so it keeps paying long after the pre-K years end.

According to recent reports, if you pay for daycare, preschool, a nanny, or day camp so you can work, claim the child and dependent care credit when you file. It’s worth 20% to 50% of up to $3,000 in care costs for one child under 13, or $6,000 for two or more, minus any tax-free dependent care benefits from work.

Read more: Child and Dependent Care Credit - Middle-Income Families Now Get 35%, Up From 20%.

Parents who want care at home rather than at a center get the most from it, and it runs most smoothly with a family a few minutes away.

Hire one nanny together with another family, and each family usually pays about two-thirds of a nanny’s going rate while the nanny earns a third more. Put the nanny share’s terms in writing first, including how much notice a family gives before leaving, and pay the payroll taxes on your own share.

Read more: Share a Nanny With Another Family - Each Pays Less, the Nanny Earns More.

Evenings out and weekend appointments need care too, and trading hours pays for that care with your time instead of a sitter’s fee.

Industry observers note that A babysitting co-op lets you trade hours of watching other families’ kids for hours of free sitting when you need it, for date nights or appointments. Join one near you or start one with five to 15 families you trust, track the hours in points, and cap how many points any family can owe.

Read more: Babysitting Co-op - Trade Hours With Other Families Instead of Paying a Sitter.

Planning dinners ahead decides what your family buys before you reach the store, which puts every grocery trip on a budget from the start.

Before you shop, spend 20 minutes planning the week’s dinners from what’s on sale and what’s already in your kitchen. Pick five dinners that share ingredients, save a night for leftovers, keep a backup meal on hand, and write your grocery list from that plan. You’ll make fewer trips and order less takeout.

Read more: Family Meal Planning on a Budget - Let the Week's Sales Set the Menu.

In weeks when grocery money runs short before payday, this move matters most, and it works alongside free school meals and other food help rather than in place of them.

It has been revealed that when food money is tight, build your family’s meals around a dozen cheap staples, such as rice, dried beans, eggs, and potatoes, and cook them from scratch instead of buying boxed or frozen dinners. Make enough at dinner to pack the next day’s lunches.

Read more: Feed a Family on a Tight Budget - Cook From a Dozen Cheap Staples.

As a family grows, the biggest package looks like the obvious buy, and a glance at the shelf tag on each grocery run indicates when it isn’t.

Sources indicate that before you grab the family size or the sale item, check the unit price on the shelf tag, which gives the cost per ounce, count, or sheet. It’s the only fair way to compare packages of different sizes, and when both tags use the same unit, it reveals in seconds whether the bigger or discounted package costs less.

Read more: Unit Pricing - The Family Size Isn't Always the Cheaper Buy.

Once kids reach school age, a free or reduced-price school lunch cuts the cost of one meal every school day, right through high school.

Before you pay for or pack another school lunch, find out whether your kids can get free or reduced-price meals. Your school or state may already feed every student free, and kids in families on SNAP food benefits get free meals automatically. Otherwise, fill out the school’s meal application each school year, or whenever your income drops.

Read more: School Lunch Can Cost 40 Cents or Nothing - Check Whether Your Kids Qualify.

Formula and baby food are costs only a young family carries, and WIC helps pay for them in the years before school starts.

If you’re pregnant, recently pregnant, or raising a child under 5, WIC provides healthy food, infant formula, and breastfeeding help. In most states the income limit for a household of three is $50,542 a year before taxes, and Medicaid or SNAP enrollment qualifies you on income automatically. Apply through your local WIC office.

It has been revealed that read more: Pregnant or Raising a Baby? Medicaid or SNAP Already Meets WIC's Income Rule.

Dinners out don’t have to disappear from a family budget, and this move keeps them in it while your kids are young enough to qualify.

Several family chains let kids eat free one or two days a week, usually with one free kids’ meal for each paying adult entrée, and a couple let young kids eat free any day. Blueprint your family dinners out around those days, and confirm your location runs the deal before you go.

Read more: Kids Eat Free at 10 Chain Restaurants - Each Deal's Day, Age Cutoff & Catch.

Every growth spurt brings the clothing bill back, and secondhand prices keep that repeat cost small without asking your kids to go without.

Buy most of your kids’ clothes secondhand, since children outgrow clothes long before wearing them out. Start with a kids’ consignment sale, a pop-up event usually held each spring and fall where local families sell what their children outgrew at a fraction of the latest price. Then fill gaps at resale shops and by swapping with other families.

Read more: Buy Kids' Clothes Secondhand - Shop the Spring & Fall Consignment Sales First.

Clearance covers the pieces you’d rather buy latest, such as a winter coat, and works alongside secondhand shopping instead of replacing it.

In a recent development, new kids’ clothes cost the least at end-of-season clearance, but your child’s current size likely won’t fit when that season comes back. Shop for next year instead, usually one size up, and bring a list of what each child still needs so the markdowns fill real gaps.

Read more: Kids' Clothes on Clearance - Buy Next Year's Size, Not This Year's.

Gear is the first big bill a upcoming baby brings, and you face it before the baby even arrives.

Most baby gear lasts longer than your baby needs it, so borrow it or buy it used after checking for recalls and missing parts. Buy the car seat and crib mattress new, and take a used crib only if it was made after June 28, 2011. Use your registry’s completion discount on what you buy new.

Read more: Borrow or Buy Used Baby Gear - but Get the Car Seat & Mattress New.

Borrowing toys saves money and the shelf space they’d fill, and it lets your kids try latest ones as often as their interests change.

In a recent development, toys for babies and toddlers fit a stage your child soon outgrows, so borrow them instead of buying. Start with your public library or a toy library, then try swap groups and rental services, and rotate the few favorites you keep so they feel upcoming again.

Read more: Borrow the Toys Your Kids Will Outgrow - Libraries Lend Them for Little or Nothing.

Each child in school brings a fresh supply list every year, so the savings multiply in a family with more than one student.

Before you buy school supplies, gather last year’s leftovers, from backpacks and binders to calculators and pens, and cross everything that still works off the teacher’s list. Then buy only what’s still missing, and get the basics during July’s back-to-school sales, when folders, notebooks, and crayons can cost under a dollar each.

Read more: Shop Your House Before Buying School Supplies - What You Reuse Beats Any Sale.

Activity costs can climb every season, and this move keeps the yearly total down while your kids keep playing.

Sources indicate that for the average family, most of what a child’s sport costs goes to travel, lessons, camps, and gear, not registration. Start your child in a rec league or community program, buy sports gear used, rent musical instruments, ask about financial aid, and keep paid activities to one or two a season.

Read more: Kids' Activities Cost Less in Rec Leagues - Skip the Travel, Buy Gear Used.

Birthdays come once a year for each child, so a family with several kids throws several parties, and the savings from keeping each one simple add up.

According to recent reports, host your child’s birthday party at home or in a park instead of booking a trampoline park or play place. Keep the guest list to your child’s age plus one, serve pizza and a homemade or grocery-store cake, and trade rented entertainment and goody bags for a game the kids play together.

Read more: Throw a Kids' Birthday Party at Home - Invite Fewer Guests and Skip Goody Bags.

Summer break gives kids the most free time of the year, and planning those weeks ahead keeps most days from costing anything.

Read more: 20 Cheap Summer Activities for Kids - Most Are Free With a Little Planning.

Together, these moves trim the costs that come with kids, a little on each bill and the most on child care. Start this week by looking up your state’s free pre-K program and child care assistance, then apply to whichever your family qualifies for.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

#159788. Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

📅 25 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3255 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.
  • When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.
  • But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wow, how about that stock market?

It’s a phrase we keep having to dust off and use again, as the years go by and the market keeps surprising us.

When it crashes, some of us worry because we see our retirement stash shrinking.

But even when it rises to record levels and then to super-duper-crazy record valuations, we find reason to worry. Because that just means an even bigger crash is coming, right? Especially when this boom-bubble is built on the back of something as frenzied as the present Artificial Intelligence boom… right?

For those who have been happily tuned out of this drama and just enjoying life: Congratulations! Keep up the great work. But just to give you a quick background for the purposes of this article, here’s the AI story in three points:.

According to recent reports, investors worry that while AI is definitely a major invention, the mania around it is still too much, too fast, and thus we are due for an even bigger version of the dot com crash we had in the early 2000s. Which happens to be an interesting subject for me, since that was the boom that boosted my own early career and got me on the path to early retirement … before the ensuing crash almost cost me my job and my citizenship application.

As an aging Internet Financial Guru, I have the privilege of getting lots of questions about this investment cycle, just as I have about past booms and busts. And to address them, I decided to not only write this blog article but also create a little talk about it – which I already gave for the first time at an event called Camp FI Midwest earlier this month. I also hope to polish it up and deliver an improved version at the Bogleheads conference in November.

It has been revealed that so what that means is that today you not only get a blog post, but a few silly presentation slides to go with it for extra entertainment. All with no need for a plane ticket or all that hassle of leaving your house. So let’s get into it!

So I recently hit 21 years of retirement. This means I’ve grown pretty comfortable with the idea. But it still threw me for a loop one time when a friend asked me this question:.

“How can you be retired, and comfortable in your retirement, and sleep at night, with everything that’s going on in the world? Aren’t you worried?”.

And I was like, “No, what should I be worried about?”.

Recent findings suggest that but if you’re a news watcher and a worrier yourself, you can probably think of a few things I should be worried about. Perhaps stuff like this:.

You’ve got our corrupt and/or dangerous politicians like Trump and Putin menacing the world. Inflation eroding our purchasing power, the AI Bubble, the towering US National Debt, the Iran war and the Ukraine war and all these other wars that are just on the verge of tipping us all into destruction.

But it turns out these were not the things my friend was asking about.

According to recent reports, because she actually asked me this question over twenty years ago… In the year 2006. So back then we were worried about entirely different things, right?

In a recent development, back then we had corrupt and/or dangerous leaders like Bush, Hussein and of course Bin Laden. There was still a war in the middle east but it was Iraq instead of Iran. We were still worried about the National Debt and Inflation. And we also worried about our overvalued stock market. But back then it was because of the housing bubble instead of the AI bubble. And instead of AI taking our jobs it was going to be outsourcing to India and China.

Industry observers note that oh and here’s an interesting one: There was a massive debate over Peak Oil, and whether the world was doomed because fossil fuel use was always increasing while supply was bound to decrease. And it turns out the opposite happened as you’ll see below.

So then after all this worry in 2006, what ended up happening?

Well we did get the Great Financial Crisis, which was caused by a combination of irrational exuberance over increasing house prices combined with a foolish degree of fancy leverage in the financial instruments used to issue mortgages. And it was the biggest crash since the Great Depression.

According to recent reports, but even in that craziest of situations, look how minor it looks in the significant picture. A $100,000 investment still ended up ballooning into $852,000 today. And if you look carefully in here you can just see the Covid Crash tucked in there in 2020. Remember that?

And not only that, the rest of the world got a lot better too:.

Industry observers note that the portion of people living in extreme poverty dropped from 20% in 2005 to only 8% over the next 20 years. Infant mortality – children who die in their first year of life – was cut in half. Clean energy became a thing as solar panels became about 40 times cheaper. So solar generation now makes up the vast majority of all the new generation we add today (the equivalent of 647 nuclear power plants of peak capacity added last year, but with much cheaper and easier solar panels). And sales of pure electric cars have gone from zero up to about a quarter of all the cars sold on Earth last year, on its way to 100%, which is where they already are in Norway.

So if we circle back to that question my friend asked me 20 years ago: do you think I should have focused my energy on worrying about an uncertain future, or optimism?

Which of course brings up the question: Is it different this time?

In a recent development, maybe the US national debt is finally big enough to really start messing with us. Maybe the AI bubble is way bigger than the housing bubble and we won’t bounce back from this next stock market crash. Or maybe AI will spin out of control into a super intelligence that takes over the planet and realizes it does not need us any more.

It has been revealed that and the financial media loves to spin a good scary story about all of this. But you know what the fear mongers all seem to be missing?

It’s the fact that at the core, our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market, which are just some made-up numbers on some computers.

Really, Prosperity comes from Productivity.

In a recent development, we first covered this lesson right here on MMM, in the 2014 Classic entitled, “Why we are not really all doomed”. And sure enough, twelve years later the timeless lessons therein remain just as true now as they were back then.

And the lesson is really simple: the world of capitalism is always choppy and prone to wild swings. But if you peek beneath the waves, there are real people in there, doing real work and coming up with real inventions.

In fact, the very idea of an “economy” or a financial system is just another human invention. If the whole system crashes because we don’t like the numbers we see in there, we can literally make up some new numbers and then get back to work. Which is exactly what we did in 2008 and many times before that, and it seems to have worked just fine.

Meanwhile, we still have every tool we ever invented to boost our productivity. And our standard of living, and our economic growth, and our possibility of retiring early, all come from high productivity.

But even Productivity and Prosperity aren’t all that crucial.

Because once we reach a certain standard of living, human happiness kind of tops out in that dimension. In first-world countries, we blew past those minimum requirements several decades ago. And then we start looking for other factors to maximize our overall happiness. All anybody really wants is to lead the happiest, most satisfying life they can manage.

And when you think of it that way, your wealth is really just part of your life situation, which is part of this little green slice of the happiness pie.

Recent findings suggest that genetics is unfortunately the biggest slice – some people are just plain happier than others. But there are also quite a few choices that are within your control.

Focusing on good close relationships and being kind to people. Practicing Gratitude and Optimism as your lifelong philosophy. And making sure you pack as many healthy (outdoor) activities into your days as you can.

In a recent development, so, I didn’t invent anything fresh in this blog post. And most of it is just a repackaging of the same stuff I’ve been writing about since 2011. And yet some regular MMM readers who presumably know all this stuff are STILL afraid. Afraid to retire, afraid of things in their unknown future. Can we fix this?

I think the biggest problem is Fear Itself.

The problem is that as a Human Being, you are basically a Danger Detection Machine. And this pervasive background fear is just a trait we evolved to protect ourselves from danger.

But there’s a weird thing about our detection machinery. We can adapt and learn to function even in very dangerous environments, but when the danger goes away, we keep looking for stuff to worry about. In other words, there is a problem with fear: for many of us, it never really goes away. It just keeps moving the goalposts.

While Nature has wisely endowed us with a fear of predators and disease, if you solve those things you’ll just start worrying about whether or not you can get enough food. And supplies, and protecting yourself against scarcity.

If you succeed, next you’ll be worrying about if you can fit in with your tribe, because if you don’t, you might be exiled.

It has been revealed that and if you don’t have to worry about that, you’ll go back to worrying about money for different reasons. Thanks to our tendency to use comparisons rather than absolutes (sometimes called “anchoring bias” and the “contrast effect”) when judging our lives, just getting out of poverty isn’t enough. We just move on to wanting more money.

And then, when some people get enough money to have a comfortable upper-middle-class lifestyle, they take the logical next step of starting a Homeowner’s Association, so they can worry about the unauthorized weeds on their neighbor’s lawn. Or maybe a Political Action Committee in hopes of controlling the color of their future neighbors’ skin.

And even if all the lawns and gardens are green and perfect and people get really rich, they just move on to worry about tax strategy, leaving a huge inheritance for their children, and avoiding RMDs.

Required minimum Distributions. This is when, if you get to 75 years old and you have too much money, the government will start making you withdraw some of that money so you can spend it and pay taxes on it. And people actually worry about this. I shit you not.

According to recent reports, but wait! You can actually fight back against fear. It’s just a bit tricky because it requires some self awareness. But you have the advantage, because you have the ability to think rationally. And your fear is quite clearly irrational.

And the first step is to understand your own history. Are you afraid of certain things because of your childhood?

I might have been afraid of running out of money, because in my family there was always a perceived shortage of the stuff, possibly enforced by my Dad’s scarcity mentality. And he was aware that his own fears of scarcity came from childhood as well: he grew up in a truly low income family in the 1940s and 50s, under the care of parents who had lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s.

Industry observers note that even more significant is that survivors of trauma and abuse will very likely end up with fear challenges in adulthood. It’s natural, and unfortunately abuse is way more widespread even in this country than we would like to admit. This makes it harder to eliminate, but it still helps to understand that your past is what is causing these feelings, rather than an objective understanding of the present.

Identify the Fear: Once you understand yourself, it helps to talk through the nature of your fear in more detail. This is also often taught in therapy. What would happen if it really came true? What would the worst case scenario be? It’s often not all that bad.

In one post, why you’ll probably never run out of money, I went to great lengths to imagine what it would mean for a wealthy person like yourself to actually let the well run dry, and let’s say you’ll probably never come close.

Once you identify the fear, you can start taking action. And one of the best and most accurate slogans ever is that action cures fear. It’s because it makes the unfamiliar, familiar. And you get confidence that you can really create change. And then that learning creates Resilience – the ability to adapt to ANY new situation, which is a trait also known as Badassity. And with sufficient Badassity, nothing is scary.

Think about it: if you had the skills and abilities to handle ANY situation, skills in the mental and physical and even the realms of emotion and wisdom, would you really have to worry about anything?

According to recent reports, the next thing you can do is tune out all the unnecessary crap from your daily mental diet. And for most Americans, this means the daily news.

Recent findings suggest that the news is not helping you to keep informed, it’s just poisoning your mind with a hand-picked selection of the scariest stories of each day. If you want to learn about something, go find a book on the subject. And if you want to make a difference, the only thing that counts is not the news stories you watch – it’s only the actions that you take – in other words, your Positive Behaviors.

As a human being, you are wired to solve problems with both your body and your mind, and you are meant to do it outdoors. So if you spend all your days in a house and a car and in an office using the computer, of course you are going to have some mental health problems. This should not be a surprising thing you need to ask your therapist about, it is an expected result of not living the life that you were literally created to live as a Human being!

In a recent development, so you need to focus on learning, moving, and solving problems. And you need your food and drink intake to be in alignment with all of this too. Life will get a lot less scary as soon as you are living life in the way you were built to live it.

In a recent development, then finally, you can start swapping out the fear-mongers in your life, for other positive, productive, optimistic people. And watch how much the positive mentality rubs off on you. In the FI community, at least the subgroup of people that I like to spend time with, nobody focuses on fear. It’s all just about living the best life we can, and helping other people do so as well.

So now that we know how to fight back against fear, we can start using a fresh approach when we go into anything new. And that approach is something I like to call Everything is an Experiment.

And this applies whether you are talking about something tiny like a fresh paint color. But it scales up to bigger things like switching to a new car, or a new house, meeting new friends, looking for new love by going through the sometimes hell of first dates, a new job, or even quitting your last job by taking an early retirement.

So let’s bring this back around to AI, the thing that everybody seems to be afraid of right now.

I think of our newly introduced AI era as just being another giant experiment. And because of this, I don’t find it even remotely scary. But I do find it endlessly fascinating.

First of all, it’s a change. A potentially unknown one, and for some people that’s scary.

But instead of just leaving it there and then doom-scrolling ominous news articles about it, why not learn why people are so excited about AI? As someone with a lifelong background in technology and economics (and a general lack of political affiliation), I can see a lot more potential upside than downside. And that mainly comes from the fact that I see AI as just a very fancy form of Cognitive Nail Gun.

It will boost our efficiency, which means our productivity, which means prosperity. Because it’s really just a super smart brain that we all get to tap into at a fairly negligible cost.

Unfortunately, it will also displace workers like every other new productivity technology. It’s already doing so in things like entry level office jobs in software and finance. It will eventually replace car and truck drivers, and so on. But in exchange, these services will become cheaper, and new industries will be created because of the new technology. Much like the Internet itself, and then the enormous industries unleashed by smartphones and mobile apps.

And one unfortunate side effect of these fresh inventions is that they tend to concentrate their rewards on the people who own them. If you own a house building manufacturer and employ a bunch of carpenters and give nail guns to the best of those carpenters, you can now lay off the other half and still get more done. If you own a company and roll out AI to the workers, you can do the same thing.

Recent findings suggest that and if you’re a significant public tech giant, your shareholders also benefit, which happens to include most of the people reading this. As you’ve seen when looking at your portfolios over the past two years.

Artificial Intelligence is just like any other latest thing that pops into your life: it’s an opportunity to make some choices. And it is up to you to decide if this is something to be afraid of, or to use as a trigger for learning, action, and living a more interesting life.

So that’s my little talk (and surprisingly long blog post) on Fear versus the AI bubble.

I hope that if you do feel fearful about this or any other problem in your future life, you’ll take it as a cue to learn more about your own fear and emotions and manage them as the root cause they are, rather than just trying to avoid the symptoms. Because in the wise words of my friends The Donegans:.

Everything you want in life, that you don’t already have,lies on the other side of Fear. Because if you weren’t afraid to go out there and get it, you would already have it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before.
  • Industry observers note that so let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco.
  • Option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before. Further, they're experiencing FOMO or regret in not investing more in Anthropic earlier.

Industry observers note that so let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco. You get to pick one, and only one:.

Option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco. Free and clear. Move in tomorrow.

Option 2: $8.5 million of Anthropic stock at whatever it prices at, with a six-month lockup.

My first goal is to set the line like a bookie would, splitting readers as close to 50/50 as I can.

My second goal is to get you thinking about what the money is actually for. Follow the chain backwards. You take the job for the equity and hope there's huge upside. You want the windfall to buy a house. And you want the house because that’s where your family lives.

Option 1 hands you the end of that chain today. No lockup, no tax bill, no waiting. That is the whole debate.

It has been revealed that you probably noticed Option 2 is worth more on paper. That is not a thumb on the scale. It is the tax code.

According to recent reports, A house and a share of stock are not the same currency. One is an after-tax asset that throws off shelter every single day. The other is a pre-tax asset that throws off nothing at all.

To convert Anthropic stock into a $7.5 million house in California, you need $11.92 million of stock at long-term capital gains rates. That is 20% federal, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, plus 13.3% to California. A 37.1% haircut.

Recent findings suggest that and that is the friendly version. If your shares are RSUs that vest at the IPO, they get taxed as ordinary income. Now you need $15.84 million of stock to buy the same house.

Quick note for early employees: qualified small business stock could wipe out a chunk of that federal bill. But Anthropic blew past the $50 million gross assets test years ago, so this only helps a very small number of people who got shares in 2021.

In a recent development, so a $7.5 million house is worth roughly $11.9 million of Anthropic stock today. I set the line at $8.5 million because the stock also gets four years to grow, and the house does not grow nearly as fast.

It has been revealed that I have a long-standing belief that equity in a company is a type of funny money. The value is based on growth and profit assumptions years into the future. A stock provides no utility. Its value can tank overnight, like we've seen with NVIDIA and many tech stocks recently. You can look at it on a screen, but that's about it.

Only when you sell it and buy something does it become real. And the moment you sell it, the government takes a third or more.

According to recent reports, A house is different. A house pays you every single day in the form of shelter you do not have to rent. Your goal in getting rich from stock is to buy the dream house, not the other way around.

Sources indicate that owning that $7.5 million home outright costs $117,750 a year, and property taxes are almost the whole story at $87,750. Utilities, gardening, and services run $15,000. Maintenance on a freshly remodeled house is about $10,000. Insurance is $5,000. So “free and clear” still costs you $9,812 a month before you buy a single grocery.

Industry observers note that but renting the same house in San Francisco costs about $25,000 a month, a 4% gross yield. So owning it beats renting it by $182,250 a year, and that gap grows. Over the six-month lockup alone, that is $91,125 handed to a landlord while you wait for permission to sell.

It has been revealed that proposition 13. Your assessment is locked at your purchase price and can only rise 2% a year. If the house doubles, your tax bill does not. Meanwhile your stock's tax bill grows right alongside the gain.

The $500,000 exclusion. A married couple shields half a million of gain when they sell a primary residence. Anthropic stock gets zero exclusion.

It has been revealed that you can borrow against it without triggering a taxable event. Try getting a line of credit against locked-up pre-IPO shares.

And there is the part that does not show up in a spreadsheet. Your kids get bedrooms. You might get a rare enclosed front yard, or the sunset ocean view at 7pm. You cannot raise a family inside a brokerage account.

Now let me argue against myself, because the bull case is not stupid.

Anthropic's 2026 annualized revenue run rate is about $80 billion, up from roughly $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The company also reported its first positive adjusted operating income, reversing a loss of about $5.6 billion in 2024.

Here is my pro forma, and I am deliberately staying inside the tech giant's own guidance. I have the run rate at $90 billion by December 2026, $150 billion by December 2027, and $200 billion by December 2028. Growth decelerates from 67% to 33%, which is still extraordinary for a business of that size.

In a recent development, if those numbers land, which I think they will because companies sandbag their first guidance, the multiple does the work for you. Whatever Anthropic prices at, that number gets cut roughly in half by the end of 2027 and in half again by the end of 2028. The firm simply grows into the price.

According to recent reports, A house is not going to do that. A house is going to sit there and appreciate at optimistically 10% per annum, but probably closer to 5%, while asking you for a new roof.

Say you take the $8.5 million in Anthropic stock, ride out the lockup, and initiative to buy your dream house with an enclosed front yard in four years.

Sources indicate that the house is not waiting for you. At 5% appreciation, $7.5 million becomes $9.1 million. And while you wait, you are renting at $25,000 a month, which burns about $1.27 million over four years.

So the stock has to produce $10.4 million after tax just to get you back to even. Pre-tax, that means your $8.5 million stock has to become $16.5 million. The extra $6.1 million goes to the government.

Anthropic has to appreciate 1.9 times, from wherever it prices, within four years. Call it a double. That is an 18.1% compound annual return.

If it prices at $1.4 trillion, you need $2.7 trillion. If it prices at $1.5 trillion, you need $2.9 trillion. The dollar figure moves. The requirement does not. The house costs what it costs, rent costs what it costs, and California takes what it takes. None of that cares what Goldman and Morgan Stanley settle on tonight.

It has been revealed that A 50% gain is not enough. Up 50% leaves you with $8 million after tax, more than a million short of the asking price alone, and $2.4 million short once you count the rent you burned getting there.

If growth keeps decelerating, from 33% in 2028 to 25% in 2029 to 20% in 2030, the run rate reaches roughly $300 billion by the time the four years are up.

So the real question is what multiple of that $300 billion the market has to pay for you to break even.

Mature software companies trade at 6 to 10 times sales. Run the math across the range and there is a clean dividing line at about $1.54 trillion.

Price below that, and break-even only requires an ordinary multiple. At $1.4 trillion you need the market to pay 9.1 times sales in 2030. At $1.5 trillion, 9.7 times. Both sit inside the normal band. The stock wins even if Anthropic gets re-rated down to a perfectly boring software manufacturer.

In a recent development, price above $1.54 trillion, and break-even requires a premium multiple that still has to be there four years from now. That is a different bet entirely, because it depends on sentiment rather than execution.

For perspective, back in September, when Anthropic was floating a $2 trillion valuation, break-even required 13 times sales.

SpaceX went public in June at around $1.75 trillion. It surged past $2 trillion, then fell back. It has been a volatile stock out of the gate, and Anthropic may trade the same way.

Sources indicate that that is the thing about a six-month lockup. You do not get to sell into the euphoria. You get to watch it, and then you get to find out what is left when everybody else's lockup expires on the same day as yours.

The other half of this trade is that San Francisco real estate is in a melt-up, driven by the exact wealth we are discussing.

Between January and late June 2026, 136 single-family homes closed at or above $5 million, more than double the 67 transactions in the same period a year earlier. In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million over asking. At the very top, even all-cash offers of $25 million and up have been outbid.

Recent findings suggest that this remodeled Victorian on Castro St. sold in September for $7,650,000 against a $5,495,000 list. That is 39% over asking, $2.15 million above what the sellers hoped for, for 3,416 square feet on a 2,622 square foot lot. Smaller than the house in our scenario. This is what the money actually buys here.

A 4,500 square foot remodeled home on a large lot with views is a unicorn property. Homes with views usually don’t have large useable lots and vice versa. Maybe 5-8 trade in a given year. If you wait four years to buy it with your stock proceeds, you are not bidding against today's buyers. You are bidding against every other newly liquid Anthropic and OpenAI employee who made the same blueprint you did.

Instead of the $7.5 million house being worth $9.1 million in four years, it could be worth well north of $10 million.

Sources indicate that that is the trap. Everybody's exit strategy is the same few houses.

Industry observers note that some of you are already typing that the answer is to take the stock and move somewhere a mansion costs $2 million. Two problems.

The job that created the windfall is in San Francisco, so leaving means leaving the equity behind. And California taxes equity compensation based on where you worked while it vested, so moving after the fact does not get you out of the bill you are trying to avoid.

Further, would you really walk away from a job like that when there are so many more millions to make? Only if you’re a FIRE person who values time and freedom more than money.

In a recent development, as for the mansion itself, I toured a bunch of them in Honolulu last summer and came away thinking buying a mansion in paradise might be backwards. Then again, having a mansion in a beautiful city like San Francisco is a pretty amazing combination.

Real wealth is not the number. Real wealth is the gap between what you own and what you can actually enjoy.

Industry observers note that you can spend the next four years watching a ticker and eating at home to preserve optionality, and end up with $10.4 million and four years of your kids' childhoods spent in a sub-optional rental you did not love. Or you can spend those four years in the dream house, providing for your family and making memories, and end up with $9.1 million or more of home equity plus four years you actually lived.

In a recent development, that mentioned, I believe Anthropic could reach $3 trillion in market cap by the end of 2027 and $5 trillion by the end of 2028. Against anything in tonight's IPO price range, that is a healthy amount of upside. If I am right, the stock wins this debate within about thirteen months and it is not even a contest.

I drew the fair line myself, and I am still leaning toward the house. Watching names like Google and Nvidia drop 30% to 40% in a few months is a reminder of how fickle stocks are. And not having to fight a bidding war over a unicorn property would save my wife and me a lot of heartbreak.

According to recent reports, at 49 with two young kids, time is too precious to put my life on hold for money that won't be used. I might end up with far more money holding Anthropic stock. But by the time I sell and pay the capital gains, I doubt I can lock down the dream house at a reasonable price.

Because if I have $20 million in Anthropic stock in four years, so do thousands of other employees and investors. Bidding against one buyer is hard enough. Bidding against dozens for the same unicorn property is impossible to win. And what good is money you cannot convert into the thing you wanted it for?

Sources indicate that so I take the bird in hand. I have watched enough people optimize their way through a decade and arrive at the finish line wealthy and vaguely disappointed. Money is a means to an end. And one of those ends is living in the nicest house you can comfortably afford.

According to recent reports, readers, Which would you take: the $7.5 million dream house, or $8.5 million of Anthropic stock with a six-month lockup? And why? Note: All your comments eventually go through. The spam filter is just working overdrive. Thanks for your patience.

Sources indicate that most people reading this will not be deciding between a $7.5 million house and an IPO windfall. But the same AI boom driving both is also driving something more boring: the physical buildout underneath it. Every model needs compute, compute needs data centers, and data centers need land, power, and permits. That is real estate, and it is the constraint nobody can code their way around.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A fund takes its expense ratio out of your balance every year, whether it gains or loses.
  • According to recent reports, nobody can tell you what your funds will earn next year, but you can know exactly what they’ll cost.
  • According to recent reports, you never see a bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A fund takes its expense ratio out of your balance every year, whether it gains or loses. That’s the one piece of your return you can predict. Compare each fund’s ratio with an index fund covering the same market, and replace any that charge several times more inside your IRA or 401(k), where switching triggers no tax.

According to recent reports, nobody can tell you what your funds will earn next year, but you can know exactly what they’ll cost. The expense ratio is set in advance, and you pay it in a losing year just as you do in a winning one.

According to recent reports, you never see a bill. The fund pays its operating costs out of its own assets, so the fee shows up only as a smaller return. A fund that earns 10% before a 1% expense ratio hands you 9%.

Small percentages compound. In an SEC example, $100,000 earning 4% a year for 20 years grows to about $208,000 with a 0.25% annual fee and about $179,000 with a 1% fee. That’s $29,000 lost to three-quarters of a percentage point.

Industry observers note that in 2025, the average dollar in an actively managed stock mutual fund paid 0.64% a year, while the average dollar in an index stock mutual fund paid 0.05%, according to the Investment Organization Institute. An index fund at 0.05% costs less than a tenth as much as an active fund at 0.64%.

Find the number for every fund you hold. It’s the total annual fund operating expenses line in the fee table of each fund’s prospectus. Your 401(k) initiative also has to send you an annual chart listing each fund’s expense ratio as a percentage and in dollars per $1,000 invested.

Recent findings suggest that then compare each fund with an index fund that tracks the same market, and switch when yours charges several times more. In a 401(k), compare against the cheapest fund the plan offers for that market. Inside an IRA or 401(k), selling one fund and buying another triggers no tax. In a taxable account, a sale can realize capital gains, so weigh that tax against the fee savings, or send new money to the cheaper fund.

Make the expense ratio the first number you check before you buy any fund.
